summary: Lower-KS2 learners name and locate at least six major bones/groups on their own body and on a diagram — skull, spine (vertebrae), ribcage, pelvis, femur (thigh bone), humerus (upper-arm bone) — pairing each scientific name with its everyday name and its job. They tie the skeleton's three jobs (support, protection, movement) to specific bones, then widen the idea of 'skeleton' using an internal-vs-external animal comparison: vertebrates have internal skeletons (usually bone; sharks' are cartilage), arthropods (insects, crabs) have exoskeletons, snails have shells, and worms have no bony or hard skeleton at all.
misconceptions: 'All animals have bones inside like us' — missing exoskeletons (insects/crabs) and animals with no bony skeleton (worms).
'The spine is one single bone' — it's a column of many vertebrae, which is why it bends.
'Scientific bone names are interchangeable/decorative' — femur and humerus name specific bones, not any big/arm bone.
'The ribcage is solid armour' — it's a cage of curved bones that also moves for breathing.
'Bigger animals have more bones' — no simple size–count relationship; focus on structure and function.
'The skeleton only helps movement' — forgetting support and protection as equally important jobs.

activities.title: Find it on you, then label it
steps: On your own body, locate and feel each target bone: run a finger down your spine to feel the separate vertebrae, press your ribcage, find the femur (thigh bone), the humerus (upper arm), the pelvis (hips) and the skull.
On a labelled human skeleton diagram, place or write the name for each of the six bones/groups: skull, spine (vertebrae), ribcage, pelvis, femur, humerus.
For each bone, say aloud the scientific name AND the everyday name together (e.g. 'femur — thigh bone'; 'humerus — upper-arm bone').

(Optional) If using an interactive skeleton, tap each bone to reveal its scientific name, everyday name and job — this is a convenience, not the thing that teaches the names; the felt location on your own body is the anchor.
activities.insight: Scientific bone names attach to real, felt locations on your own body, not just to labels on a picture; femur and humerus name specific bones, not any big or arm bone.

activities.title: Match each bone to its job
steps: Match or write the job of each bone: which bones SUPPORT (hold the body up and give it shape), which PROTECT organs, and which enable MOVEMENT with muscles.
Give a worked example for each job: femur supports your weight; skull protects the brain; ribcage protects the heart and lungs; humerus moves your arm when muscles pull on it.
Notice that some bones do more than one job, and name all three jobs rather than only 'holding you up'.

(Optional) If using an interactive skeleton, a 'three jobs' filter can recolour bones to show at a glance which ones SUPPORT, which PROTECT and which MOVE — treat this as a sorting aid, then still state the job in your own words.
activities.insight: The skeleton has three important jobs — support, protection AND movement — and each can be tied to specific bones with examples.

activities.title: Do all animals have bones inside?
steps: Compare animals by how their body is held up and protected: a beetle or crab has a hard OUTER casing (an exoskeleton); a snail has a shell; a worm has no bony skeleton inside or out.
Sort several animals into groups: internal skeleton, exoskeleton, shell, or no hard skeleton.

Explain what is the SAME and what is DIFFERENT between a crab's exoskeleton and your skeleton (same jobs — support, protection and movement with muscles attached; different design — outside versus inside).

(Optional) A lift-the-flap 'do all animals have a skeleton like mine?' reveal — e.g. a beetle wearing its skeleton on the outside and a snail's shell — can prompt the comparison, but any side-by-side comparison serves the same goal.
activities.insight: 'Skeleton' means the structure that supports and protects a body, which can sit inside or outside; not all animals have internal bones like ours.

activities.title: Build-and-name self-check
steps: Assemble or label a skeleton by dragging/writing each bone name onto the correct bone, then check against the correct placement.
Match each bone to its job (support / protect / move).
Categorise a set of animals by skeleton type (internal / exoskeleton / shell / no hard skeleton) and check your sorting.
activities.insight: Active labelling and sorting can consolidate precise naming and the internal/external distinction, and can reveal any remaining gaps.

checkQuestion: A crab and a beetle are hard on the OUTSIDE, but you are soft on the outside and hard on the inside. Do they have bones like you, just in a different place? What is the same and what is different about how their bodies are held up — and what are the THREE jobs your own skeleton does?
checkAnswer: A crab and beetle don't have bones inside — they have a hard outer casing called an exoskeleton that supports and protects them from the outside; your skeleton does similar jobs but is on the INSIDE. The three jobs of your skeleton are support (holding your body up and giving it shape), protection (the skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs), and movement (bones work with muscles). Same jobs, different design — inside versus outside.
